opening.title: Remove required work before polishing instructions
keyPoints: Measure the actual workload first
Compare preprocessing, queries, and updates together
Keep required output and numeric semantics unchanged
opening.narration: Optimization begins with a correct reference and a workload. If a program repeatedly scans the same data, an index or precomputed summary can remove far more work than changing one instruction in the scan. But construction costs, update frequency, and memory use still count. A one-query dataset that changes constantly may favor the original scan. State which behavior must remain identical, including overflow rules and error handling, before comparing performance. This chapter separates algorithmic work counts from measured running time: fewer operations can be strong evidence for an idea, but hardware and the rest of the workload determine the actual improvement.

question.prompt: Why can an index be slower overall even though each lookup is faster?
question.answer: Its construction, update, and memory costs may exceed the saved query work for the actual workload.

opening.title: An index replaces repeated equality tests with maintained counts
keyPoints: Six records answer three frequency queries
The direct method makes eighteen comparisons
The index is built once and queried three times
opening.narration: The fixture contains two, four, two, seven, two, four. Counting each requested value with a fresh scan performs six comparisons three times, for eighteen. Building a map of counts visits the six records once; the three lookups then produce the same total of six matches. The program prints these operation counts and verifies the result. It does not measure elapsed time or claim that a map lookup costs one machine instruction. A small direct scan can still be faster because map nodes allocate memory and require pointer traversal. The useful lesson is how repeated work changes and which setup cost must be included.

opening.title: Batching changes call count while preserving item order
keyPoints: Ten items are grouped into batches of at most four
Three calls replace ten per-item calls
The final partial batch must still be sent
opening.narration: The baseline would send ten items with ten separate calls. Our model appends items into a batch of four, flushes each full batch, and finally flushes the remaining two. The sink receives the exact original string in order, while the number of modeled calls drops to three. The empty check in flush avoids an unnecessary fourth call. This is a batching mechanism demonstration, not a network speed measurement. A real service must also cap waiting time: if it waits forever for four items, the last two may never leave. Batch size and flush policy therefore belong to the observable latency and memory contract.

question.prompt: Why is the final flush required even though the loop already flushes full batches?
question.answer: The total count may not be divisible by the batch size. Here the last two items would otherwise remain unsent.

code.model: An in-memory sink models batching; no syscall cost or speedup is measured.

opening.title: Prefix summaries trade update cost for query cost
keyPoints: A leading zero makes half-open ranges uniform
prefix[right] − prefix[left] answers a range
Changing old data invalidates later prefix entries
opening.narration: The source uses half-open ranges: left is included and right is excluded. A prefix vector begins with zero, so prefix at position k means the sum of elements before k. Subtracting prefix[left] from prefix[right] then handles ordinary, full, and empty ranges with one formula. This is useful when many queries reuse stable data. If one element changes, every later prefix can become stale; the old fast query is now quickly wrong. A maintained tree or a direct scan may fit a different update pattern. Numeric bounds must also ensure the stored sums and their subtraction stay representable.

mechanism.title: Compiler options are part of the experiment’s contract
keyPoints: Ordinary optimization preserves permitted behavior
Some flags change floating-point or target assumptions
Record the exact build, not only “release”
mechanism.narration: A compiler can inline calls, combine operations, remove dead work, or vectorize a loop when the language rules permit it. The source loop need not look the same in assembly. But some options change assumptions, such as allowing less strict floating-point transformations or requiring instructions unavailable on older processors. An apparent improvement may therefore come with changed results or portability. Record the complete relevant build configuration and verify the required outputs under it. A release label alone does not identify the program being measured. Fix undefined behavior rather than treating one favorable optimized result as a guarantee.

question.prompt: Why might enabling a target-specific instruction option make a binary unsuitable for another machine?
question.answer: The generated instructions may require CPU features absent on that target. Performance and deployment requirements must be evaluated together.

mechanism.title: Layout should serve the fields a hot loop actually uses
keyPoints: A 32-byte record may contain one hot 8-byte field
A dense field array can reduce irrelevant traffic
Other operations may prefer complete records together
mechanism.narration: The source layout model considers eight thousand one hundred ninety-two records of thirty-two bytes each, while a hot pass reads only one eight-byte field. The complete records occupy two hundred fifty-six kibibytes; the isolated field array occupies sixty-four. That is a footprint calculation, not a guaranteed fourfold speedup. The original data may already be cached, other fields may be needed by the next operation, and splitting records can complicate ownership and updates. Compare the full access pattern before changing layout. Useful bytes per transfer can explain a measurement, but does not replace the application's completion metric.

question.prompt: Why does reducing a modeled footprint fourfold not imply a fourfold runtime improvement?
question.answer: Other work, existing cache residency, reconstruction, synchronization, and memory behavior can limit or offset the benefit.

mechanism.title: Allocation reduction creates new lifetime choices
keyPoints: reserve can avoid repeated growth
Reusable buffers can retain excessive capacity
An arena reclaims objects together
mechanism.narration: Repeated small allocations can add overhead, but each replacement technique changes the lifetime model. Reserving a known vector capacity can reduce reallocations while still requiring a sensible upper bound. Reusing a buffer avoids acquisition work but may retain a huge capacity after one unusual request. A scoped arena makes many allocations cheap and reclaims them together, which fits only when their lifetimes can end together. Do not keep raw observers into storage that a later growth or arena reset invalidates. An optimization should make the required ownership clearer, not save allocation calls by introducing dangling references.

question.prompt: What new resource risk appears when a server reuses its largest-ever request buffer forever?
question.answer: One unusually large request can cause long-lived memory retention. Reuse needs a capacity and shrink or eviction policy.

mechanism.title: Branch removal can perform work that the branch avoided
keyPoints: Predictable branches can be inexpensive
Computing both outcomes may add work
Both candidate memory accesses must still be valid
mechanism.narration: A branch that is almost always taken can be cheaper than calculating both possible results. For irregular input, a different arrangement may help the processor, but only measurement can establish that for the actual distribution. More seriously, rewriting a guarded load into two unconditional loads can access an invalid address even if a later selection discards its value. Source-level validity comes before branch-count reduction. Compare representative input patterns and inspect what the compiler generates rather than assuming a conditional expression is automatically branchless or faster. The cost belongs to the resulting dependency and memory behavior, not the spelling alone.

question.prompt: Why can calculating both sides of a choice break correctness?
question.answer: One side may contain an operation that is valid only when its condition holds, such as reading an optional buffer. Discarding its result does not undo the invalid access.

closing.title: Optimization verification needs adversarial equivalence cases
keyPoints: Keep the independent reference implementation
Test empty, boundary, and invalid inputs
Include updates when cached summaries are maintained
closing.narration: An optimized implementation should be compared with a straightforward reference across cases that expose different behavior. Empty ranges catch off-by-one assumptions. Large allowed values test arithmetic bounds. Invalid ranges test error contracts. If the optimization caches summaries, mutate the underlying data and verify the documented invalidation or update path. A performance run on one all-positive fixture can miss a wrong subtraction, stale index, or different rejection rule. Keep correctness checks separate from the timing interval when appropriate, but do not remove them from the experiment. Faster wrong answers do not satisfy the same workload.

question.prompt: What test is essential after introducing a reusable cache or precomputed summary?
question.answer: A change to its source data followed by another query, verifying the documented update or invalidation behavior.

closing.title: Accept an optimization only with its full tradeoff
keyPoints: What work disappears?
What memory or maintenance cost appears?
Which workload benefits?
What evidence preserves the old contract?
closing.narration: A useful optimization review names the removed work and the new costs. The frequency index eliminates repeated scans but adds construction and storage. Batching reduces call count but changes waiting and buffering. A compact layout can reduce irrelevant memory traffic but complicate operations that need full records. These are concrete tradeoffs, not reasons to reject optimization. State the workload where the change helps, verify equivalence, measure the chosen boundary, and document any new invariants. If the input distribution or update frequency changes later, maintainers should know which assumption to re-evaluate before preserving an old optimization by habit.

question.prompt: What should a maintainer know before keeping a prefix index after the workload changes to frequent updates?
question.answer: Its query advantage depends on reuse between updates; rebuilding or maintaining prefixes may now dominate the workload.
